_meta.title: AI Transparency Index
_meta.lede: How openly the major AI providers let the public see what their AI costs — in dollars, in data, and in water and energy. We grade transparency, not the underlying footprint: whether a real figure is findable at all, and who had to surface it. 'Not disclosed' is a finding, not a gap to paper over.

axes.label: Environmental impact
axes.note: Capacity-weighted water & energy disclosure across known AI data center sites. Scored below.

axes.label: Pricing
axes.note: Five dimensions of what a provider tells you about what you are buying, all read from primary sources. Scored below. Providers tell you the price and when it will change; none tells you what you get for it.

axes.label: Data practices
axes.note: Four dimensions of what a provider tells you about what happens to your conversations. Scored below. Business customers are opted out of training by default; consumers are opted in and must find the toggle.

_meta.methodology: We grade three independent axes — pricing, data practices, and environmental impact — separately, and never average them into one score. Four-state system: 🟢 Transparent (the company discloses it itself) · 🟡 Partial (a real figure is public, but only via a regulator, utility, or watchdog — not the company) · 🔴 Opaque (nothing public) · ⚪ Not yet assessed (we haven't checked yet — which is not the same as opaque). For environmental impact specifically: we track each provider's known AI data center sites and grade every site on water/energy disclosure, then roll them up into a capacity-weighted average — bigger sites carry more weight. That means a large opaque site can't hide behind a small transparent one, and one bad site doesn't sink an otherwise-open provider either. Every grade links to its sources — 122 of 122 across all three matrices (42 environmental, 40 pricing, 40 data practices), every URL checked. The pricing axis was defined and scored on 2026-08-25 across five independent dimensions — API rate card, consumer allowance, consumer context window, price-change notice and model-retirement notice — graded separately and never averaged, on the same 4-state scale. Its provider set deliberately differs from the environmental one: it covers the eight companies selling AI directly to consumers or developers. The data-practices axis was defined and scored on 2026-08-25 across five dimensions — whether the training default is stated, whether an opt-out is documented, whether a retention period is published, whether human review is disclosed, and (added 2026-08-29) whether advertising use is disclosed — read from each provider's consumer-facing documents. All three axes are now scored, and all three remain separate: a provider can be open about billing and silent about water, and several are.

grade_legend.label: Partial — public only via regulator, utility or watchdog

caveats: Site coverage is currently 12 sites across 7 providers and expanding over time — that reflects our research pace, not a judgment on any provider we haven't listed yet. Early-stage campuses with no meaningful operating capacity yet (e.g. Meta's Hyperion, the Stargate expansion sites) are tracked but shown without a capacity weight until they're running. Pure-play colocation landlords (e.g. Equinix, NTT, CyrusOne) aren't scored here yet — they publish fleet-wide efficiency rather than per-AI-site figures, and need their own treatment.
Most 🟡 grades today exist only because of local advocacy groups and utility-records work — not because any law requires the company to disclose. That gap is itself part of the story.
Grades are re-verified periodically, not continuously — a site can move between checks.
This is Legerly's independent read of public information, not a regulatory finding. Tell us if we got something wrong.

A known limitation of the AI-vs-total split column, stated rather than hidden: for the three AI-only companies (xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic) it is not an independent measurement. Their total IS their AI footprint, so the column can only repeat what site-level disclosure already says — if they published a total, the split would be satisfied trivially. Read those three cells as one finding about publishing nothing, not two. The column does real work only for the hyperscalers, where AI competes with search, cloud and everything else inside the same meter.

detail.title: Disclosure quality by dimension
detail.note: A closer look at how complete each company's own environmental reporting is, across six disclosure dimensions. This lens grades a company's self-reporting rather than the 'can the public find out at all' question the site scores above answer — so here 🟢 means good disclosure, 🟡 partial, 🔴 none or poor. We grade what each company DISCLOSES about the AI compute it controls, not the footprint itself. Rented-vs-owned rule: each company is graded only on what IT publishes, regardless of who owns the building — so a renter that stays silent has disclosed nothing, while one that publishes facility detail gets credit. That rule used to name OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI together as silent; on 2026-08-29 we corrected it, because xAI is not. It publishes a Memphis site with turbine counts, permit dates, emissions-control specification and a water-recycling plant with a projected annual volume — which moved two of its cells to 🟡. What it still does not publish, and what this table grades, is a single figure for the water or electricity Colossus actually uses. Anthropic and OpenAI remain silent on the environment in the ordinary sense: a full-text search of Anthropic's Transparency Hub returns zero hits for water, energy, carbon, emissions, climate and electricity. Cross-board: no company separates AI-specific from general data-center footprint AT FACILITY LEVEL — Google is the one partial exception, publishing AI-specific per-prompt energy, carbon and water while leaving the AI share of its 13,562 Mgal data-centre withdrawal unknowable, which is why its cell is 🟡 and not 🔴. None discloses indirect (power-generation) water — LBNL estimates indirect ≈ 12× direct — and there is no U.S. federal water-disclosure mandate as of mid-2026. TWO DATES TO WATCH, one voluntary and one legal. On 23 June 2026 the UN Secretary-General launched the AI Environmental Transparency Initiative, asking every major AI company to disclose its full carbon, water and land footprint and to power its data centres with renewables by 2030; as of this check, more than two months on, no provider on this table has been named as having signed up, and none of these grades has moved because of it. California's SB 253 is the harder deadline: Scope 1 and 2 reporting is due from November 2026 for large companies operating in the state, with Scope 3 not due until 2027.
caveats: We grade DISCLOSURE quality, not true environmental performance. A low grade means opacity, not necessarily high impact — a genuine closed-loop site (e.g. Abilene) may use little water yet still score 🔴 for not publishing numbers.

Withdrawal ≠ consumption, and direct ≠ indirect. No company discloses indirect (power-generation) water, which LBNL estimates at ~12× direct — so every 'water positive' claim understates the true system footprint.

Some gradings are genuinely ambiguous and are flagged, not silently resolved: Meta's site-level cell now sits between 🟡/🟢 — it reports electricity and emissions per facility but no per-site water, and we graded the missing metric rather than the present ones; Microsoft's ‘water positive’ claim is still aggressive, but for a narrower reason since Aug 2026 — it now publishes withdrawal per location while keeping consumption in aggregate.
Conflicting figures are shown as ranges, not picks — e.g. Google Council Bluffs 2024 ≈ 1.0B gal consumed / 1.3B potable / 1.4B withdrawn depending on source and metric.

The xAI/OpenAI/Anthropic non-disclosure finding was re-verified on 2026-08-25 against reporting from Aug 2026, not left resting on the Dec 2025 trackers — a verified absence expires too. The underlying fact, that no company environmental report exists, is directly checkable from the absence of any such document. California's SB 253 requires Scope 1 and 2 reporting from large companies operating in the state starting November 2026, so these rows may finally move within a year; classifying the bulk as Scope 3 would delay most of it to 2027.

pricing.title: Pricing transparency — by dimension
pricing.note: What a provider tells you about what you are buying. Same 4-state scale as the page above, applied to five independent dimensions and never averaged. THE HEADLINE FINDING: providers are good at telling you the price and when it will change, and almost uniformly silent on what you get for it. Six of eight commit to a quantified price-change notice and five of those land on exactly 30 days with a cancel-before-renewal right — the most standardised disclosure in the industry. Set against that, THREE OF EIGHT publish no usage allowance whatsoever — Anthropic, Google and xAI — and a fourth, DeepSeek, we have not been able to read. That count moved on 2026-08-31 and it moved because we went looking, not because anyone published anything: OpenAI, Microsoft and Mistral all turned out to publish absolute figures we had graded them 🔴 for. FOUR OF EIGHT NOW PUBLISH SOMETHING AND ALL FOUR BOUND A SINGLE FEATURE — Codex, Copilot’s Agents/Vision/Voice, Flash answers, Computer — WHICH IS THE REAL FINDING: not that providers cannot quantify, but that the quantified surface is never the one you are buying. Perplexity remains the most usable of the four: “Consumer Max plans start with 10,000 credits a month”, with “100 credits equals $1” and typical consumption published by task class — the only allowance figure on this table a reader can do arithmetic with. It covers one product surface on one tier, which is why it is 🟡 rather than 🟢, and it is still more than the other seven manage. The 2026-08-29 re-read also found THREE providers publishing a consumer context window, not one — OpenAI per tier (27K to 128K instant), Google per tier (32k / 128k / 1M) and Anthropic per model (200K / 500K / 1M). Put those together and the pattern is not incapacity: providers quantify the size of ONE conversation precisely, and all but one refuse to say HOW MANY you get. Note the provider set differs from the environmental axis above: this table covers the eight companies that sell AI to consumers or developers directly, so Amazon and Meta are absent and Perplexity, Mistral, DeepSeek and Microsoft appear. IT ALSO EXCLUDES Z.AI, WHICH PUBLISHES MORE ABOUT ITS ALLOWANCE THAN ANY PROVIDER ON THIS TABLE — absolute credit caps on two windows, the credit formula, the per-model multipliers and a token conversion. It was added to Legerly's price tracking on 2026-08-30 and has not been graded on any axis here, because grading it means reading its privacy, retention and environmental disclosures rather than assuming them. Until that happens, read “seven of eight” as a statement about these eight and not about the market: the strongest counter-example to this axis is one we have not yet scored.

grade_legend.label: Published by the provider, and usable
Published but incomplete, unquantified, or late

caveats: This axis grades DISCLOSURE, not value for money. A plan can be excellent and still score 🔴 here for not saying what it includes, and a cheap plan gets no credit for being cheap.

Price-change and model-retirement notice have now been read directly on all eight providers' own terms and docs — no cell on this axis rests on a secondary source. The single remaining ⚪ is Microsoft's API rate card, which is not graded because Copilot is sold as a subscription with no per-token price to publish; that is a different business model, not a disclosure failure.

The allowance finding comes from Legerly's own plan-limits data, where every plan carries a provenance value and a source. It is a count, not an impression — but it is only as good as its last re-read, and on 2026-08-29 it gained a second published figure: Perplexity Max's 10,000 credits a month, which had been on Perplexity's help centre since 2026-08-06 and which we had missed. Re-count against the provider's own pages rather than trusting the stored total. Updated again 2026-08-30, when Z.ai's three GLM Coding tiers were added to the price data with full credit allowances — taking the count from 25-of-27 to 26-of-31. The absolute number barely moved and the RATIO weakened materially, which is the number to quote: 96% became 84% while the sentence stating it did not change. Both corrections came from looking again, neither from a provider publishing anything new.

Price-change notice turned out BETTER than we expected when we started this axis, and it is recorded that way. Both OpenAI and Anthropic give consumers 30 days and make increases effective at next renewal so the subscription can be cancelled first. An axis that only found bad news would not be evidence.

Corrected 2026-08-29: this axis used to say OpenAI was alone in publishing a consumer context window. It never was. Google's Gemini Apps limits page carries a per-plan table and Anthropic's help centre a per-model breakdown, and the Internet Archive shows Google's table was live eleven days before we recorded it as unpublished. Two cells moved 🔴→🟢 as a result. The mistake ran in the providers' disfavour, which is the direction an index like this one has the least excuse for.

The four context-window cells flagged as unverified earlier on 2026-08-29 have since been re-read on consumer-facing pages, and all four held at 🔴 — but the check was worth running twice over. Two of them had been cited against the wrong document: the Perplexity and DeepSeek cells proved a claim about CONSUMER plans by linking to API documentation. Mistral, DeepSeek and xAI all publish per-model context windows to developers (256k, 1M and 500k respectively) while telling consumers nothing, and the notes now say so instead of asserting a bare absence.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates for every model published on its own developer pricing page; re-verified against that page on 2026-08-24, when gpt-5.6-sol had moved $5/$30 → $4/$20.

allowance.note: Corrected 2026-08-31, and it is the second time this axis has been wrong against OpenAI in the harmful direction. This cell said "the only absolute consumer figure any provider publishes is OpenAI’s, and it is a feature sub-limit" — by then Perplexity, Microsoft, Mistral and Z.ai all published one, and OpenAI itself published far more than the Thinking sub-limit we credited it with. On developers.openai.com OpenAI publishes a per-model, per-plan table of local messages per FIVE-HOUR window for Codex — GPT-5.6 Sol 10-100 on Plus, 50-500 on Pro 5x, 200-2,000 on Pro 20x, with Terra and Luna rows too — plus a credits-per-1M-tokens rate card carrying cached-input rates, and "GPT-5.6 usage averages 5-30 credits per message". Two consequences worth stating. First, this is the only place OpenAI has ever quantified the base its "5x/20x more usage" marketing multiplies: the Pro columns are exactly 5x and 20x the Plus column. Second, it names a WEEKLY window and never sizes it — "Additional weekly limits may apply", and unhedged in the help centre, where a banked reset "refreshes your 5-hour and weekly Codex usage windows". 🟡 not 🟢 because every figure bounds Codex and the agentic features sharing its allowance, not ordinary chat: the ChatGPT Free FAQ and the Pro tiers article still name no window of any kind. The deletion of the general cap in August 2026 stands; what is new is that the silence is narrower than we said.
allowance.source: developers.openai.com/codex/pricing; help.openai.com Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan

context_window.note: The one thing that got BETTER. OpenAI's plan table publishes a per-plan context window for every consumer tier — Instant 27K/54K/54K/128K and Reasoning Varies/256K/256K/400K across Free/Go/Plus/Pro — and it is on the pricing page itself rather than buried in support. It bounds one conversation, not how many you get, so it does not close the allowance gap. This cell used to add that OpenAI was alone in publishing a consumer context window; that was never true. Google publishes a per-plan table and Anthropic a per-model one, and both were live when we wrote it.

price_change.note: Consumers do better than developers here. The consumer Terms of Use commit that 'if we increase our subscription prices, we will give you at least 30 days' notice and any price increase will take effect on your next renewal so that you can cancel'. The business/developer Services Agreement is shorter and blunter: 'Price changes on the Pricing Page will be effective fourteen days after they are posted.'
price_change.source: OpenAI Terms of Use + Services Agreement (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: The strongest retirement commitment of any provider: a published deprecations page promising minimum notice of at least 6 months for generally available models and at least 3 months for specialized variants, with preview models explicitly carved out at around 2 weeks. Quantified, tiered, and stated as a floor.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own pricing docs and re-verified there on 2026-08-24. Also handled an intro-rate expiry honestly: Sonnet 5's $2/$10 launched as an introductory rate, and rather than letting it lapse quietly the pricing page states the scheduled 2026-09-01 rise to $3/$15 will not occur.

allowance.note: Across the 31 consumer plans Legerly tracks, from 9 providers, 21 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier graded here is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Two things about that ratio, both of which cut against this table rather than for it: it has weakened from 26-of-27 since 2026-08-25 — because we looked harder, not because anyone published anything — and three of the ten exceptions are Z.ai’s GLM Coding tiers, which these eight rows do not cover at all. Anthropic's four consumer plans all sit in that 26. Max is sold as '5x/20x more usage than Pro' with Pro itself unquantified, and the Consumer Terms say plan limits are 'described in the order process' while the terms themselves specify none.
allowance.source: claude.com/pricing; Anthropic Consumer Terms; Legerly plan-limits.json

context_window.note: Corrected 2026-08-29 — this cell said no consumer figure existed, and that was wrong. Anthropic publishes absolute numbers for what a paid subscriber gets, per model: “Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 support a 1M token context window on all paid plans when chatting with Claude”, Opus 4.8 / 4.7 / 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 get 500K, and “outside of these models, Claude's context window size is 200K.” It goes further than most by stating the figures separately for Claude Code and Cowork, and by naming where a tier changes the answer — Pro users must enable usage credits for the 1M window on Opus models in Claude Code. Structured per model rather than per plan, which is the honest shape when the limit genuinely depends on the model. The one real weakness is location: it is a help-centre article, not the pricing page a consumer compares plans on.
context_window.source: Anthropic help centre, “How large is the context window on paid Claude plans?” (read directly)

price_change.note: Quantified on both sides and read directly. Consumer Terms: fees will not change during a current term, and 'if these changes result in an increase in the fees payable by you, we will inform you at least 30 days in advance', with the increase applying at renewal so it can be cancelled first. Commercial Terms: updated rates take effect 'the earlier of 30 days after the updates are posted or Customer otherwise receives Notice'.
price_change.source: Anthropic Consumer Terms + Commercial Terms (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: A published lifecycle page committing to at least 60 days' notice before retirement for publicly released models — a shorter floor than OpenAI's, but paired with something no one else does: a forward 'not sooner than' retirement date for every ACTIVE model, most of them a year or more out, plus a complete deprecation history back to 2024. In practice that is more usable than the 60-day floor implies.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own Gemini API pricing page, re-verified 2026-08-24 — at which point 3.6 Flash and the new 3.7 Flash had been put on a half-price promotional rate with a stated end date of 2026-12-31. Dating the promo is the right behaviour; an undated promotional rate is a trap.

allowance.note: Across the 31 consumer plans Legerly tracks, from 9 providers, 21 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier graded here is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Two things about that ratio, both of which cut against this table rather than for it: it has weakened from 26-of-27 since 2026-08-25 — because we looked harder, not because anyone published anything — and three of the ten exceptions are Z.ai’s GLM Coding tiers, which these eight rows do not cover at all. Google's five consumer tiers are sold as '2x/4x/20x higher than standard limits', with its own footnote clarifying that the base is non-AI subscribers. It also reserves the right to change limits 'without notice, including due to capacity constraints'.

context_window.note: Corrected 2026-08-29 — “no per-plan consumer context window published” was wrong. The Gemini Apps limits page carries a plain three-row table: no AI plan 32k tokens, AI Plus 128k tokens, AI Pro and AI Ultra 1 million tokens. That is the same shape as OpenAI's disclosure — absolute, per tier, on the provider's own help page — and it is accompanied by an explanation of what the number means in practice (“up to 1,500 pages of text or 30,000 lines of code”). Verified against the Internet Archive as live on 2026-08-14, eleven days before the pass that recorded it as unpublished, so this is our correction rather than a change at Google. Note the contrast within this same row: Google quantifies the context window precisely and leaves the usage allowance entirely unquantified.
context_window.source: Google, “Gemini Apps limits & upgrades for Google AI subscribers” (read directly)

price_change.note: Verified on Google's own Google One terms, which govern its AI subscriptions: “We will give you at least 30 days’ prior notice of a price increase before you are charged.” It also publishes the remedy if it misses that — “if you are given less than 30 days’ prior notice, the change will not apply until the payment after the next payment is due” — which is a stronger construction than most peers, because it says what happens when the commitment is broken rather than only stating the commitment.
price_change.source: Google One Additional Terms of Service (read directly)

model_retirement.note: A deprecations page exists, which puts Google ahead of five providers here, but it carries NO quantified commitment. Shutdown dates in the table are explicitly 'the earliest possible dates on which a model might be retired', with a promise only to 'communicate the exact shutdown date with advance notice' — advance notice of unspecified length. A date you cannot rely on and a notice period with no number.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own model docs and re-verified there 2026-08-24, including the higher above-200k-context tier.

allowance.note: Across the 31 consumer plans Legerly tracks, from 9 providers, 21 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier graded here is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Two things about that ratio, both of which cut against this table rather than for it: it has weakened from 26-of-27 since 2026-08-25 — because we looked harder, not because anyone published anything — and three of the ten exceptions are Z.ai’s GLM Coding tiers, which these eight rows do not cover at all. All five xAI consumer tiers are in that count. Re-read 2026-08-31 across x.ai/pricing, x.ai/grok and help.x.com’s X Premium page specifically to ask whether xAI names a usage WINDOW, after OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Perplexity all turned out to. It does not. Every reference to Grok volume is relative and unwindowed — "higher rate limits", "increased usage limits on Grok", "higher limits on Grok" — with no base, no period and no reset. Of the nine providers tracked, xAI is the only one that names neither a number nor a window. This is 🔴 and not ⚪ because all three pages rendered and were read; help.x.com served a Cloudflare interstitial first and the real page on a retry.

context_window.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29. The consumer pricing page states no context window, and neither does the Grok consumer FAQ. xAI does publish per-model context in its developer documentation — the models page lists 500k tokens — but that is the API product. Nothing tells a SuperGrok subscriber what their conversation limit is. Same rule as Mistral and DeepSeek: publishing the model spec to developers is not telling the consumer.
context_window.source: x.ai/pricing and the Grok consumer FAQ, against docs.x.ai models (all read directly)

price_change.note: Verified on xAI's own consumer Terms of Service: “If prices increase, we will provide 30 days’ notice, and the new price will apply at your next renewal, allowing you to cancel if you disagree with the change.” Worth noting against the environmental axis above, where xAI is 🔴 on all six dimensions: the axes are genuinely independent, and a company can be opaque about water while being straightforward about billing.
price_change.source: xAI consumer Terms of Service (read directly)

model_retirement.note: Publishes retirement events properly but commits to no notice period. Its May 15 2026 retirement page names every retired slug, the redirect target, the exact cut-off time, and — usefully, and more than most disclose — the pricing impact: requests to a retired slug after the date are billed at the replacement model's rate. That is real operational disclosure. What is missing is a policy: nothing states how much warning the next retirement will carry, so you cannot plan, only react.
model_retirement.source: xAI model retirement migration guide (read directly)

rate_card.note: The clearest case on this table of a published price that is not the price. Perplexity publishes per-token Sonar rates — but they EXCLUDE a $5–14 per 1,000 requests fee which, for ordinary chat-shaped use, exceeds the token cost itself. A user pricing their usage off the published rate card would materially understate their bill. The number is disclosed; the cost is not.

allowance.note: Corrected 2026-08-29, and it breaks what used to be this table's cleanest line. Perplexity publishes an absolute consumer allowance: “Consumer Max plans start with 10,000 credits a month.” It also publishes what a credit is worth — “100 credits equals $1” — and typical consumption by task class: light 100–350 credits, complex 350–950, heavy 875–2,275, mega 2,400–9,800. That is the only figure on this axis a consumer can actually do arithmetic with, and it makes Perplexity the sole provider not 🔴 in this column. It is 🟡 rather than 🟢 because of what it does not cover: the number applies to Computer, Perplexity's agent product, and “Consumer Pro plans do not start with a set monthly amount.” Ordinary search and chat volume stays unquantified — Pro merely gets “a high volume of daily searches.” So one product surface on one tier is quantified and the rest of the plan is not. Note the page also reserves the right to change it: “credit pricing, task ranges, and monthly allowances may change and can vary by promotion, region, or plan.”
allowance.source: Perplexity help centre, “How Credits Work on Perplexity” (updated 2026-08-06), plus the Pro and Max plan articles

context_window.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29 against the consumer help centre rather than the API docs this cell used to cite — which was the wrong document to prove a claim about consumer plans. The plan articles for Pro and Max, and the AI-models collection, describe model access and search volume in qualitative terms and never state a context window for any tier. Perplexity routes between third-party models whose individual context windows are published by their makers, which makes the consumer's effective limit depend on a routing decision Perplexity does not expose.
context_window.source: Perplexity help centre — Pro, Max and AI-models articles (read directly)

price_change.note: The only major provider whose price-change commitment carries no number. Its Terms of Service say only that “any price changes or changes to your subscription plan will take effect following reasonable notice to you.” Reasonable is not a period you can plan around, and it is unenforceable in any practical sense — the same unquantified-promise pattern that keeps Google's deprecation page at 🟡. Every other provider here except DeepSeek states a figure.

model_retirement.note: No notice-period policy, no forward retirement dates, and no lifecycle page — retirements surface as changelog entries, in at least one case recorded as already having happened (“Gemini 3.1-flash-lite-preview has been retired”). A log of what was removed is not notice of what will be. There is a structural reason worth stating fairly: Perplexity resells other providers' models, so some retirements are forced on it upstream and outside its control. That explains the position; it does not make the user any better informed.
model_retirement.source: Perplexity docs changelog (read directly); no lifecycle policy found

rate_card.note: Not applicable in the same form and therefore not graded: Copilot is sold as a subscription and Microsoft publishes no per-token consumer rate card of its own, reselling model access rather than pricing it directly. Grading this 🔴 would punish a different business model rather than measure disclosure.

allowance.note: Corrected 2026-08-31. Microsoft publishes a per-plan limits table and it carries real absolute numbers: Agents 25 tasks per month on Premium, Vision 10/10/15 minutes per day and Voice 30/30/60 minutes per day across Personal/Family/Premium, and 60 AI credits per month on Personal and Family with a worked example ("asking Copilot to summarize my inbox would deduct one AI credit"). It also distinguishes the two mechanisms in writing: "feature limits are the total number of times you can use a specific feature within a specific timeframe, while AI credits are monthly usage allotments." 🟡 rather than 🟢 for one reason, and it is the same reason as Kimi in Legerly’s price notes: the numbers stop exactly where the money is. Chat on every tier is "Extensive use", and the credit line on Premium — the paid upgrade — is "Extensive usage beyond standard credit limits" against a Personal/Family figure of 60. A company that quantifies voice to the minute is not unable to quantify; it is choosing which number is commercially sensitive.
allowance.source: support.microsoft.com, AI credits and limits for Microsoft 365 subscriptions (updated July 2026)

context_window.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29 against consumer-facing pages rather than assumed. No context window is published for any Copilot consumer tier, and Microsoft's own guidance sidesteps the number entirely: a support page advises keeping referenced content “to around 80,000 words or less” for Copilot to work effectively, which is a rule of thumb about document length, not a stated limit. Prompt character limits (raised to 4,000 and 8,000) are published, which bounds what you can type rather than what the model can hold. A consumer cannot learn how much Copilot will actually keep in view.
context_window.source: Microsoft Copilot consumer pages and support guidance (read directly)

price_change.note: Verified in the Microsoft Services Agreement §9.j: at least 15 days' notice by email or other reasonable manner before a price change, applied at the next renewal, with a cancel-before-it-takes-effect right, and fixed-term locked-in prices exempt. Graded 🟢 because it is published, quantified and usable — but it is half the 30 days five other providers commit to, and that difference is stated here rather than hidden behind the badge. This axis grades disclosure, not generosity.

model_retirement.note: Consumer Copilot does not expose or version the model you are talking to, and Microsoft publishes no model-retirement notice policy for it. What it does announce, ad hoc through blog and message-centre posts, is FEATURE retirement — Deep Research and Podcasts both retired in consumer Copilot on 2026-08-18. Graded 🔴 rather than ⚪ (unlike the rate-card cell, where per-token pricing genuinely does not exist for this product) because the gap here is real and consumer-affecting: the model underneath can change without the user being told, or being able to tell.
model_retirement.source: Microsoft Copilot plans + retirement announcements; no model-lifecycle policy found

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own pricing page and re-verified 2026-08-24. Also the only provider here publishing a student price ($5.99/mo) rather than routing students through an eligibility wall.

allowance.note: Corrected 2026-08-31. Mistral publishes exactly one absolute consumer figure and it is not in the plan table: "Flash answers: 200 / day on Team vs. 150 / day on Pro", in an FAQ answer to a different question. The comparison table itself is relative throughout — messages "Up to 6x free", web searches "Up to 5x free", image generation "Up to 40x free" — all against a Free base that is never quantified anywhere, with "Subject to fair usage limits" attached to the unlimited rows. So the only number a reader can act on is the one Mistral did not put in the table it built for comparing plans. 🟡 not 🔴 because the figure is real, published and dated; 🟡 not 🟢 because it covers one feature and the plan’s actual message allowance stays a multiple of an unknown.
allowance.source: mistral.ai/pricing, plan comparison table and FAQ

context_window.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29 on the fully rendered pricing page: the Vibe plan comparison contains no context-window figure at all. Mistral does publish per-model context windows in its developer documentation — its models overview lists them per model, and Mistral Medium 3.5 and Small 4 are documented at 256k — but nothing connects those numbers to what a Free, Pro or Student subscriber gets in Vibe, or says which model a given tier actually runs. The figure exists for developers and not for the consumer, which is the gap this column measures.
context_window.source: mistral.ai/pricing (rendered) and docs.mistral.ai models overview (both read directly)

price_change.note: Verified on Mistral's own consumer terms, and it commits the same 30 days as the majors in both its rest-of-world and EU versions: “If we increase our prices, we will give you at least thirty (30) days’ notice and any price increase will take effect the next time your subscription renews … so that you can cancel if you do not agree.” The EU version adds that notice is sent by email to the account address.
price_change.source: Mistral ROW + EU consumer Terms of Service (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: The surprise of this axis. Mistral publishes a model lifecycle policy with a quantified notice period per stage — General Availability 6 months, Public Preview 1 month, Labs 1 month, third-party models 1 month — and states that the model stays accessible throughout the deprecation window. Its 6-month GA commitment equals OpenAI's and beats Anthropic's 60-day floor. It also maintains a dated deprecation table with retirement dates and named replacements. The smallest provider on this table has among the best disclosure on it.
model_retirement.source: Mistral model lifecycle policy + deprecation table (read directly)

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own API docs and re-verified 2026-08-24, including its peak/off-peak split.

allowance.note: Downgraded from 🔴 to ⚪ on 2026-08-31, which is a correction to US, not a change by DeepSeek. This cell was graded off the shared aggregate sentence rather than off a DeepSeek page — exactly the failure this index recorded against xAI on 2026-08-29. Checked properly: deepseek.com renders as a JavaScript shell (599 characters of text to a plain fetch), chat.deepseek.com returns an empty 202, and the only readable DeepSeek documentation is the API rate-limit page, which covers per-account CONCURRENCY — a different thing from a consumer usage window and not quotable as one. No consumer-facing limits page was read, so no absence can be asserted. DeepSeek also has no paid consumer tier, so there may be no allowance to publish; that too is unestablished rather than known. To close this, open chat.deepseek.com in a logged-in browser.
allowance.source: deepseek.com; api-docs.deepseek.com rate limit and FAQ pages

context_window.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29. DeepSeek publishes a context length prominently — its API pricing page states 1M, with a 384K maximum output — but that is a model and API specification. Nothing on the consumer side states what chat.deepseek.com gives you or whether it differs from the API. DeepSeek also has no paid consumer tier, so there are no plans to differentiate; the honest reading is that the consumer question is never addressed rather than that a plan allowance was withheld. Held 🔴 on the same rule applied to Mistral and xAI: a developer-facing model spec is not a statement to the consumer.
context_window.source: DeepSeek API pricing/models documentation and the consumer site (both read directly)

price_change.note: Warned, but barely. DeepSeek told developers on 2026-08-06 that a significant API price increase was coming, WITHOUT stating the new rate or the date; the increase landed on 2026-08-16, roughly ten days later, at 3–4.5× the previous rates. A warning with no number and no date is better than a silent change and materially worse than the 30 days OpenAI and Anthropic commit to. We had recorded the warning before it landed, and it landed as recorded.
price_change.source: DeepSeek API docs + pricing announcement; Legerly prices.json history

model_retirement.note: Announces retirements with a forward date and reasonable lead time, but has no published policy. Its updates page carried “the two legacy API model names, deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner, will be discontinued in three months (2026-07-24)” — three months of warning, dated, on its own docs. Better lead time than its price-change behaviour, where a rise landed roughly ten days after a warning that named neither rate nor date. Held at 🟡 because one well-handled instance is not a commitment.
model_retirement.source: DeepSeek API docs updates page (read directly)

data_practices.title: Data practices — by dimension
data_practices.note: What a provider tells you about what happens to your conversations. Same 4-state scale, four independent dimensions, never averaged. THE HEADLINE FINDING IS AN ASYMMETRY, AND THE PROVIDERS DOCUMENT IT THEMSELVES: at OpenAI, Anthropic and Mistral the paying business customer is opted OUT of model training by default while the consumer is opted IN and must find a toggle. OpenAI's own help page states both halves — consumer ChatGPT “improves by further training on the conversations people have with it, unless you opt out”, while “by default, we do not train on any inputs or outputs from our products for business users”. Anthropic's Commercial Terms say flatly that “Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services”, against consumer terms that train unless you opt out. Same company, same models, opposite default — the difference is which customer had the leverage to negotiate. This axis grades DISCLOSURE, so a provider that states its practice plainly scores well even when the practice is unflattering; the asymmetry above is recorded here rather than as a column, because grading it would mean grading conduct, which this index deliberately does not do. A fifth dimension, ADVERTISING USE, was added on 2026-08-29, and its finding is a substitution: only two providers answer the question a consumer actually has — are my conversations used to choose the ads I see? OpenAI says yes and documents how; Google says no and says it will tell you if that changes. The other six answer an easier, adjacent question instead — whether they SELL or SHARE your data with advertisers — and those are different things. A provider can truthfully say it never sends your prompts to an advertiser while still reading those prompts to pick the ad it shows you itself. A second pass on 2026-08-29 enumerated the HUMAN REVIEW column instead of sampling it, and three of its five 🔴 cells fell: Anthropic has a help article titled “Who can view my conversations?”, OpenAI discloses human review of reported content, and Microsoft states outright that it “manually review[s] some of the results against the underlying data” to improve its AI. Only DeepSeek and Perplexity disclose nothing — and Perplexity's own Privacy & Data collection answers every adjacent question except this one. Every cell on this axis is now graded. The 2026-08-29 pass corrected six of them, five in providers' favour — what changed was our reading, not their policies.

grade_legend.label: Stated plainly, in the consumer-facing policy
Stated but hedged, incomplete, or hard to act on

caveats: We grade what the CONSUMER-FACING documents say — the privacy policy a normal user would actually reach, plus each provider's own data-use FAQ where one exists. A practice disclosed only in an enterprise contract or a developer changelog does not count as telling the consumer.

A 🔴 on ‘human review’ means the consumer privacy policy does not disclose it, not that no human review happens. The absence of the disclosure is the finding; the underlying practice is not something we can observe.

Defaults change, and this axis rots faster than the environmental one. Anthropic moved consumer chats into training with an opt-out during 2025; any of these positions can move with a policy update that nobody announces.

On 2026-08-29 we re-read every source on this axis and corrected six cells — three for xAI, two for Perplexity, one for OpenAI. In each case the provider's disclosure had been there all along and we had missed it, mostly because a page failed to load for us and we recorded the silence as theirs. We publish the corrections rather than quietly restating the grades, because an index that grades disclosure has to disclose its own errors.

The advertising column grades DISCLOSURE, not whether a provider shows ads. “We do not engage in targeted advertising”, stated plainly, is 🟢 — DeepSeek and Mistral both earn it that way, and so does OpenAI for documenting an ads product in detail. What loses marks is answering a narrower question than the one asked.

training_default.note: States it plainly in its own data-use help page: ChatGPT “improves by further training on the conversations people have with it, unless you opt out.” No hedging, no ambiguity — you are training data by default and the page says so. Contrast the same page on business products: “by default, we do not train on any inputs or outputs from our products for business users, including ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, and the API.”
training_default.source: OpenAI data-use help page + privacy policy (both read directly)

optout.note: A documented, free opt-out: “you can opt out of training through our privacy portal by clicking on ‘do not train on my content’”, after which “new conversations will not be used to train our models.” Note the limit it states honestly — the opt-out is forward-looking only and does not reach conversations already used.

retention.note: Published in the privacy policy under a plain “Retention” heading, with numbers attached: anything you delete is removed “within 30 days”, Temporary Chats are “automatically deleted within 30 days”, and the reasons it keeps data longer are listed rather than gestured at — a policy ban, a lawful subpoena, financial record-keeping, and the audit record of your own deletion request. One real gap: content already de-identified for model training sits outside that 30-day window and no period is given for it at all, where Anthropic states five years for the same thing. We previously recorded this as unassessed. That was our error rather than a change at OpenAI — the same text was live on the day we last checked.
retention.source: OpenAI privacy policy §4 Retention, plus the delete-and-archive help article (both read directly)

human_review.note: Corrected 2026-08-29 from 🔴. OpenAI does disclose human review, on a consumer help page whose summary line reads “Learn how OpenAI uses automated systems and human review to identify harmful or policy-violating content”, and which states that for reported content “we use a combination of automated systems and a trained team of experts to review these reports.” It is 🟡 and not 🟢 because of scope: the disclosure covers content that has been reported or flagged, and says nothing about whether people read conversations in the ordinary course of improving the model — which is the question a consumer opting into training is actually asking. The Data Controls FAQ adds that Temporary Chats “may be reviewed only to monitor for abuse”, again without saying by whom.
human_review.source: OpenAI help centre, “How we identify problematic content on our services for individuals”, plus the Data Controls FAQ

advertising.note: Answers the question a consumer actually has, and answers it in detail. Ads arrived in ChatGPT for Free and Go users — the test began in the US on 9 February 2026, with no ads on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise or Edu, and none shown to accounts identified as under 18. The help page names the signals: selection uses “the context and intent of your current conversation”, and with personalisation on it may also use “Past chats and memory”. It states what advertisers get (“aggregated, non-identifying information”, never “your chats, chat history, memories, or personal details”), how long ads data lives (“up to 30 days” after you clear it), and that ads are not eligible near “personal health, mental health, or politics”. You can turn personalisation off, or switch to an ads-free Free plan with lower limits. Disclosure this specific is rare here — and it describes an unflattering practice, which is exactly what a disclosure grade should reward.
advertising.source: OpenAI, “Ads in ChatGPT” help page, plus the privacy policy (both read directly)

training_default.note: Stated in one sentence in the consumer privacy policy: “We may use your Inputs and Outputs to train and improve Anthropic AI models, unless you opt out through your account settings.” Worth knowing that this is a changed default — consumer chats were moved into training with an opt-out during 2025 — which is why this axis carries a caveat that positions move.

optout.note: Opt-out is in account settings and free, and the policy says so in the same sentence that discloses the default rather than burying it in a separate document.

retention.note: The most specific retention disclosure of the eight, with different periods for different states and all of them numbered: deleted conversations “removed immediately from your conversation history and automatically deleted from our back-end within 30 days”; if you allow training, data is kept de-identified “for up to 5 years in our model training pipelines”; feedback submissions retained 5 years. It also states the exceptions — legal, dispute, Usage Policy enforcement.
retention.source: Anthropic privacy centre, model-training article (read directly)

human_review.note: Corrected 2026-08-29 — “no disclosure of human review” was wrong, and Anthropic has an entire consumer help article whose title is the question: “I would like to input sensitive data into my chats with Claude. Who can view my conversations?” It states, explicitly scoped to consumer products, that “we automatically de-link your data from your user ID (like your email address) before any review” and that “access is limited to a small number of personnel involved in model training.” It names the safeguards — filtering and obfuscation of sensitive data, no profiling, no marketing, no sale — and the carve-out: “if our safety classifiers flag your conversations, they may still be used to improve our internal trust and safety models … or advance our safety research”, which applies even to users who have opted out of model improvement. Answers who, under what controls, and what still happens if you opt out.
human_review.source: Anthropic help centre, “Who can view my conversations?”, plus the consumer privacy policy

advertising.note: Addresses advertising only in the narrow sense of marketing its own products: “You can opt-out of sharing your personal data for targeted advertising to promote our products and services, and we will honor global privacy controls.” That is a real, actionable control. What the policy never says is whether your conversations with Claude are, or could be, used for advertising of any kind. Anthropic does not appear to run an ads product, which would make the answer an easy no — but a consumer cannot learn that from the document, and the point of this column is that they should not have to infer it.

training_default.note: The Gemini Apps privacy notice is explicit that chats are used to improve models, and pairs it with a warning most providers do not print: “please don't enter confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services.” Telling users plainly not to trust the box with secrets is unusual and counts in its favour here.

optout.note: Gemini Apps Activity is a documented consumer control, free, with the consequences spelled out. Google is also candid about the limit of the control, which most providers would omit: with Activity off, “Google still uses your chats to respond to you and help protect Google, our users, and the public, including with help from human reviewers.”

retention.note: Numbers, defaults and options all published: Gemini Apps Activity auto-deletes on a default of 18 months, changeable to 3 months, 36 months or indefinite. Reviewed feedback and its associated conversations are “retained for up to 3 years, disconnected from your Google Account.” A consumer can work out how long their data lives.

human_review.note: Discloses human review plainly and, unusually, discloses that it continues after you turn Activity off: reviewed conversations are retained up to three years, disconnected from your Google Account, and Google tells you not to enter anything you would not want a reviewer to see. This cell used to add that Google was the ONLY provider telling consumers that humans read some conversations. That was wrong: Anthropic has a help article dedicated to the question, and OpenAI and Microsoft both disclose human review in narrower terms. Google's disclosure is still the most complete of the four — it is the only one that ties review to a retention period and to the state of your privacy settings.
human_review.source: Google, Gemini Apps Privacy Hub (read directly)

advertising.note: The clearest answer on the table, from the company with the most to gain from the opposite one. The Gemini Apps privacy hub carries the question as its own heading — “Do you use my Gemini Apps chats to show me ads?” — and answers it: “Your Gemini Apps chats are not being used to show you ads. If this changes, we will clearly communicate it to you.” It then discloses the carve-out rather than hiding it: if you add products to a Google shopping cart from Gemini, or pay through Google Pay in Gemini, that cart, order and transaction data “is used in accordance with the Google Terms and Privacy Policy … including for personalization and ads (depending on your settings).” Your chats do not feed ads; commerce you transact inside Gemini does; Google says both halves out loud.
advertising.source: Google, Gemini Apps Privacy Hub (read directly)

training_default.note: The consumer privacy policy states that its models are trained on “your Input and Output, subject to your opt-out”, and separately carves out what it will not touch: “we do not use this Third-Party Content to train our models.” Plain enough that a consumer knows where they stand.

optout.note: “You can opt-out of this processing at any time through your user preferences on your Mistral AI Account” — documented, free, and in the account rather than behind a support request.

retention.note: Publishes real, numbered retention periods, but for the wrong things from a chat user's point of view: contracts and commercial licences for 5 years after termination, technical support data 5 years. No retention period for conversations. Graded 🟡 rather than 🔴 because the disclosure discipline is clearly there — it just has not been applied to the thing a consumer cares about.

human_review.note: Does not disclose human review of conversations for model improvement, but is unusually specific about internal access generally: data kept for legal periods “will not be accessed or used by any member of our teams … except to fulfil our legal obligations or in case of dispute”, and access is limited to “authorised members of our teams who need to access your personal data, strictly to perform their jobs.” Adjacent to the question, not an answer to it.

advertising.note: States the non-practice explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred: “Mistral AI has not ‘sold,’ ‘shared,’ or engaged in ‘targeted advertising’ … in the preceding 12 months, including of any consumer that we know is under 18 years old.” Two honest limits: the wording borrows US state-law definitions and looks back twelve months rather than committing forward, and a separate list of business purposes for service providers does include “Providing advertising and marketing services.” Still a plain answer to a plain question, from the smallest provider here.

training_default.note: Discloses the practice but hedges the one detail that decides whether it applies to you: “in some markets, this data can help train our AI models in Microsoft Copilot unless you opt out.” Which markets is not stated, so a consumer cannot place themselves. It also discloses that Copilot “uses prompts and related data to provide and improve services, including relevant advertising” — consumer prompts feeding ad targeting, stated in the privacy statement itself. We used to add that no other provider here disclosed that; since OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT that is no longer true, and OpenAI now documents it in more detail than Microsoft does.

optout.note: An opt-out is referenced in the same market-dependent sentence, but no mechanism is documented in the privacy statement itself and no indication is given of where a given user stands. There is a privacy dashboard for viewing and deleting Copilot activity, which is a different control from opting out of training.

retention.note: No retention period for Copilot conversations. The statement lists the criteria it uses to decide retention and then says “actual retention periods can vary significantly” — a description of a process rather than a disclosure of an outcome. A consumer learns nothing about how long their chats live.

human_review.note: Corrected 2026-08-29 from 🔴. The privacy statement does disclose it, in one sentence that names both the practice and its purpose: “Our processing of personal data involves both automated and manual (human) methods … to build, train, and improve the accuracy of our automated systems – such as AI - we manually review some of the results against the underlying data.” That is a plainer statement of human review for AI improvement than OpenAI manages. It stays 🟡 because it is Microsoft-wide rather than Copilot-specific: the reader cannot tell whether their Copilot conversations are among the data reviewed, and the statement covers every Microsoft product at once.

advertising.note: Discloses the practice — Copilot “uses prompts and related data to provide and improve services, including relevant advertising” — which is the substance of it, and which for a long time made Microsoft the only provider here admitting that consumer AI prompts feed ad targeting. It is 🟡 because that sentence sits inside an omnibus privacy statement covering every Microsoft product, where “advertising” appears 85 times about everything from Xbox to Bing. Nothing tells a Copilot user which signals are used, what controls exist for Copilot specifically, how long ads data is kept, or which markets it applies in. The practice is disclosed; the shape of it is not.

training_default.note: Asserts the right without stating the default. The policy tells you that you have “the right to opt-out of using your Personal Data for training our models or optimizing our technologies”, which implies you are opted in, but never says so. It is explicit only about the uncontroversial half — “we may obtain publicly available Personal Data via online sources to train our models.” An opt-out right disclosed without the default it reverses leaves the consumer guessing.

optout.note: The right is stated; the mechanism is not. No setting, portal or process is documented anywhere in the privacy policy, which makes it a right you would have to ask for rather than a control you can use.

retention.note: Entirely qualitative. “We retain Personal Data for as long as necessary to provide our Services”, retention periods “will be different depending on the amount, type and sensitivity”, and data is kept “for as long as you have an account.” Not one number anywhere in the section.

human_review.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29 and still 🔴, this time by enumeration rather than assumption. The privacy policy contains no human-review disclosure of any kind — no reference to personnel, staff, reviewers or manual review of conversations — and DeepSeek operates no consumer help centre in which one could appear; the only FAQ surface is API documentation, which does not address it either. A reader cannot learn whether anyone at DeepSeek reads their chats.
human_review.source: DeepSeek privacy policy and its API FAQ (both read directly; no consumer help centre exists)

advertising.note: The bluntest statement of the eight, in capitals in the original: “NOTE WE DO NOT ENGAGE IN TARGETED ADVERTISING, ‘SELL’ PERSONAL DATA OR USE PERSONAL DATA FOR ‘PROFILING’ OR OTHERWISE ENGAGE IN AUTOMATED PROCESSING OF PERSONAL DATA TO MAKE DECISIONS THAT COULD HAVE LEGAL OR SIMILARLY SIGNIFICANT IMPACT ON YOU.” It covers the practice itself, not merely selling data to someone else, which is the distinction most of this column turns on. Worth recording that DeepSeek is 🔴 on retention and on human review and 🟢 here: these dimensions are independent, and a provider can be plain about one thing and silent about another.

training_default.note: Never states the default for your chats. The privacy policy lists a purpose — “improve or create services and products, including our AI models” — which tells you your data may reach a model without telling you whether it does by default or whether you can stop it. Tellingly, it is precise where it wants to reassure: “we do not use the content of emails to create, train, improve, or fine-tune AI models.” The specificity available for email is not extended to conversations.

optout.note: The control exists and is documented: “AI Data Retention is enabled by default” for Free, Pro and Max users, and you turn it off under Account settings → Preferences. The limits are stated honestly too — opting out applies only going forward, and “previously collected training data cannot be deleted or removed.” It is 🟡 rather than 🟢 because none of that appears in the privacy notice a normal user actually reaches: that document sets out three separate opt-outs for advertising and not one for model training. The toggle is also named for retention while what it governs is training, which is an easy thing to misread in the provider's favour.
optout.source: Perplexity help centre, “Data Collection at Perplexity”, read against the privacy notice

retention.note: A number does exist, in the help centre rather than the policy: personal information is kept “as long as your account is active”, and on deletion is “removed from our servers within 30 days.” Held at 🟡 for three reasons — the privacy notice itself is entirely qualitative, the same pattern graded 🔴 elsewhere on this table; there is no retention period for a single thread short of deleting your whole account; and Perplexity states that training data already collected cannot be removed at all. We previously could not load the page that carries this. It loads fine — that was our tooling, not their disclosure.
retention.source: Perplexity help centre retention and self-serve deletion articles

human_review.note: Re-verified 2026-08-29 and still 🔴. Neither the privacy notice nor any of the nine articles in Perplexity's own “Privacy & Data” help collection mentions human review, reviewers, personnel access or manual inspection of conversations. The collection covers what data is collected, how long it is kept, how to delete it and whether third-party model providers train on it — every adjacent question except this one.
human_review.source: Perplexity privacy notice plus all nine articles in its Privacy & Data help collection (read directly)

advertising.note: Perplexity does advertise, and says so — its 8 July 2026 notice update added “first-party advertising measurement” and states that “we do not sell your personal data or send your queries, prompts, or conversation content to advertisers.” The notice documents three separate advertising opt-outs, more than it offers for anything else. The gap is the one that decides most of this column: not sending your prompts to advertisers is not the same as not using your prompts to choose which ad Perplexity shows you, and that second question is never answered. Advertising appears 18 times in the notice without resolving it.

training_default.note: Corrected. We previously called this the clearest non-disclosure on the axis, and that was simply wrong: the consumer FAQ the privacy policy points to answers the question directly — “We may use your content and interactions with Grok (e.g., prompts, searches, and other materials you submit) along with Grok's responses to train our models.” It stays 🟡 rather than 🟢 for one reason: “may” leaves the default unstated. You can work out that you are opted in from the fact that the control offered is an opt-out, but the company never says so outright.
training_default.source: SpaceXAI (xAI) consumer FAQ, plus the privacy policy that points to it

optout.note: Corrected, and it is one of the better-documented opt-outs on this table: Settings → Data Controls → “Improve the model” on mobile, Settings → Data → “Improve the Model” on Grok.com. The limits are stated rather than buried — it applies only to new conversations, feedback you volunteer can still be used for training afterwards, and if you use Grok without logging in, outside the EU and UK, there is no opt-out at all. That last admission is one most providers here do not make.

retention.note: Genuinely good, and worth crediting given the row above: “if you choose to delete any or all of your conversations or if you choose to delete your account, we will delete the data within 30 days”, with Private Chat conversations “deleted from SpaceXAI systems within 30 days.” A number, applied to a named control, with the legal and safety exceptions stated.

human_review.note: Corrected. The consumer FAQ asks “Do humans view my conversations?” and answers it: “A limited number of our authorized personnel may review your conversations with Grok for specific business purposes, including improving model performance, investigating security incidents and potential misuse of our services, and complying with our legal obligations.” The purposes are named, not just the fact of review. On this dimension only Google discloses more.

advertising.note: The consumer FAQ answers a neighbouring question well: “We do not sell your data or share it with third parties for marketing or advertising purposes. Thus, there is nothing you need to do to opt out.” But sharing your data with advertisers and using your data to target ads at you are different things, and only the first is addressed. The privacy policy's single advertising reference is a cookie purpose — cookies may “deliver relevant content and targeted advertising” — which concerns the website rather than Grok conversations. Whether your chats with Grok could ever select an ad is not stated either way.
advertising.source: SpaceXAI (xAI) consumer FAQ and privacy policy (both read directly)

site_level.note: Re-read 2026-08-25 against the 2026 Environmental Report (FY2025) — our previous note was a reporting cycle out of date and understated this. Google publishes withdrawal, discharge AND consumption for 36 named data center locations across eight countries (US, Ireland, Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, Chile, Canada), plus an aggregated “other locations” bucket — up from 24 locations. It remains the most complete site-level disclosure of any provider, and it is stronger than Microsoft's on the two points that matter: Google publishes consumption, not just withdrawal, and the table sits inside the third-party limited-assurance scope rather than outside it.
site_level.source: Google 2026 Environmental Report, “Water use by data center location” (read directly)

ai_split.note: Re-checked 2026-08-25: the per-prompt figures are unchanged — median Gemini Apps text prompt at 0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO₂e and 0.26 mL water, measured as of May 2025. The 2026 report adds that per-prompt energy and carbon fell 33× and 44× over twelve months, but facility reporting still does not split AI from general load, so the AI share of that 13,562 Mgal data-center withdrawal remains unknowable.

comparability.note: Resolved 2026-08-29 by reading Google's own methodology paper (arXiv 2508.15734) rather than the report. We used to record that the per-prompt figures had “no published denominator”. The truth is sharper: THERE IS NO DENOMINATOR BY CONSTRUCTION. The paper defines the “median Gemini Apps text prompt” by taking the average energy per prompt for each model, ranking the models by that value, and finding the model that serves the 50th-percentile prompt — “the average energy/prompt is defined as the energy of the median Gemini Apps text prompt on that day.” So “median” describes the MODEL, not the prompt, and the headline number is an average across every prompt that model served, whose size distribution is never characterised. It cannot be converted to a per-token rate even in principle, which is why a reader cannot apply it to their own usage. Two things keep this at 🟡 rather than 🔴, and both are to Google's credit: the methodology is published in full, and the paper reports BOTH boundaries rather than the flattering one — 0.10 Wh / 0.12 mL on the narrow “Existing Approach” against 0.24 Wh / 0.26 mL on the “Comprehensive” one, a 2.4× spread from a single measurement, with the larger figure the one Google quotes publicly. The irony is worth recording: the same paper faults OpenAI's 0.34 Wh for giving “no explanation of the measurement boundary or methodology … making it impossible to compare with other estimates”, and notes that Mistral states its own figure per 400-token response. Google identified the failure precisely and then shipped a version of it.
comparability.source: Google, “Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale” (arXiv 2508.15734), read directly; plus the 2026 Environmental Report

replenishment.note: Replenished 78% of the freshwater it consumed in 2025 (9,947 Mgal consumed, 7,717 Mgal replenished), against a stated goal of 120% by 2030 — a real number, published, and trending up. Still graded 🟡 because replenishment is reported by watershed but returned water often sits in different watersheds than those drawn down, so the fleet figure does not mean local supply was made whole.
replenishment.source: Google 2026 Environmental Report, freshwater replenishment table (read directly)

energy_source.note: Achieved ~65% global average carbon-free energy in 2025 (up from 64%), and at least 80% CFE in 9 of 22 grid regions — reported by region, which is better than any peer. But it is still a market-based accounting method, and total emissions are now 62% above the 2019 base year, up from the ~51% we recorded last cycle. The trend line and the headline percentage point in opposite directions.

energy_source.note: Moved 🔴→🟡 on 2026-08-29. What was wrong was the last sentence — that xAI “discloses no energy mix.” On its own Memphis pages it now states what powers the site: temporary turbines “have now been permanently removed from the Electrolux site”; it applied for 15 permanent turbines in January 2025, approved by the Shelby County Health Department on 2 July 2025, and expects to need only 12, “eventually only be used for backup power”; it is “securing additional power from the grid”; and the permitted turbines carry SoLoNOx dry-low-emissions and selective catalytic reduction bringing NOx “to 2 ppm.” Still 🟡, not 🟢: that is equipment and permits, not an energy mix — no generation split, no MWh, no Scope 1/2 inventory. Reported turbine counts still differ across sources, so we quote xAI's own numbers as its claims rather than as findings.
energy_source.source: xAI (SpaceXAI) Memphis “Fact v. Fiction” read directly; SELC; EPA applicability determination
